notes:
Alkanes (C$_n$H$_{2n+2}$)

  • Prepared by Wurtz reaction (2R-X + 2Na $\to$ R-R, works best for identical R), decarboxylation of sodium salts of carboxylic acids with soda lime, and catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes/alkynes (Ni/Pt/Pd).
  • Free radical halogenation proceeds via initiation-propagation-termination; relative reactivity of H: 3° > 2° > 1°. Combustion: $C_nH_{2n+2} + \dfrac{3n+1}{2}O_2 \to nCO_2 + (n+1)H_2O$.

Alkenes (C$_n$H$_{2n}$)

  • Prepared by dehydration of alcohols (conc. H$_2$SO$_4$, 443 K, Zaitsev's rule — more substituted alkene major) and dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH.
  • Electrophilic addition: HX adds by Markovnikov's rule (H to carbon with more H, X to carbon with fewer H, via more stable carbocation). In presence of peroxides, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch effect, free-radical mechanism) — only for HBr, not HCl/HI.
  • Ozonolysis: alkene + O$_3$ then Zn/H$_2$O gives two carbonyl compounds — used to locate the position of the double bond.
  • Markovnikov example: propene + HBr $\to$ 2-bromopropane (major).

Alkynes (C$_n$H$_{2n-2}$)

  • Acetylene from CaC$_2$ + H$_2$O. Terminal alkynes (-C$\equiv$CH) are acidic (sp C-H), give white/red ppt with ammoniacal AgNO$_3$/Cu$_2$Cl$_2$ — distinguishes terminal from internal alkynes.
  • Addition of 2 mol HX/X$_2$/H$_2$ across the triple bond; controlled hydrogenation with Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/BaSO$_4$ + quinoline) gives cis-alkene; Na/liq. NH$_3$ gives trans-alkene.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons

  • Benzene: planar, hexagonal, all C-C bond lengths equal (139 pm, between single 154 pm and double 133 pm) due to resonance/delocalisation of 6 $\pi$ electrons; resonance energy $\approx$ 152 kJ mol$^{-1}$ explains unusual stability (Hückel's rule: planar, cyclic, $(4n+2)\pi$ electrons, n = 1 for benzene).
  • Electrophilic aromatic substitution: nitration (HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ $\to$ NO$_2^+$), halogenation (X$_2$/FeX$_3$), Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation (RCl or RCOCl/anhyd. AlCl$_3$).
  • Directive effect: -OH, -NH$_2$, -R, halogens (o,p-directing; halogens deactivate despite this via $-I$ dominating $+R$); -NO$_2$, -COOH, -CN, -SO$_3$H (m-directing, deactivating).
  • Carcinogenic/toxic: benzo[a]pyrene (polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon).

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 3-4 questions from Hydrocarbons — expect one each on Markovnikov/peroxide effect, ozonolysis product identification, benzene EAS directive effects, and a naming/isomer count question.

questions.q: Wurtz reaction of 2 mol of CH$_3$CH$_2$Br with sodium metal in dry ether gives
questions.explanation: Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halide molecules: 2C$_2$H$_5$Br + 2Na $\to$ C$_2$H$_5$-C$_2$H$_5$ (n-butane) + 2NaBr.

questions.q: Addition of HBr to propene in the presence of benzoyl peroxide gives mainly
questions.explanation: Peroxide promotes a free-radical mechanism (Kharasch/anti-Markovnikov effect) only with HBr, so Br attaches to the terminal (less substituted) carbon giving 1-bromopropane.

questions.q: Ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene followed by treatment with Zn/H$_2$O gives
questions.explanation: 2-Methylbut-2-ene is (CH$_3$)$_2$C=CH-CH$_3$; ozonolysis cleaves the C=C giving (CH$_3$)$_2$C=O (acetone) and CH$_3$CHO (acetaldehyde).

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes but-1-yne from but-2-yne?
questions.explanation: But-1-yne is a terminal alkyne with an acidic $\equiv$C-H; it gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO$_3$, while but-2-yne (internal) does not.

questions.q: Controlled hydrogenation of an alkyne using Lindlar's catalyst gives
questions.explanation: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/BaSO$_4$ poisoned with quinoline) adds H$_2$ syn to the triple bond, stopping at the cis (Z) alkene.

questions.q: The C-C bond length in benzene (139 pm) is intermediate between a single bond (154 pm) and a double bond (133 pm) because
options: of steric strain in the ring
of delocalisation of the 6 $\pi$ electrons over all 6 carbons (resonance)
benzene has alternating single and double bonds that do not interact
questions.explanation: Benzene is a resonance hybrid of Kekulé structures; the $\pi$ electrons are delocalised equally over all six C-C bonds, making all bond lengths equal and intermediate in length.

questions.q: According to Hückel's rule, an aromatic monocyclic compound must be planar, cyclic and have
questions.explanation: Hückel's rule requires a planar, fully conjugated cyclic system with $(4n+2)$ delocalised $\pi$ electrons (n = 0,1,2,...); benzene has n = 1, giving 6 $\pi$ electrons.

questions.q: Nitration of toluene with conc. HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ gives mainly
options: 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene directly in one step at room temperature
questions.explanation: -CH$_3$ is an activating, ortho/para-directing group (electron release by hyperconjugation/+I), so nitration gives predominantly o- and p-nitrotoluene.

questions.q: Which of the following groups is meta-directing and deactivating on a benzene ring?
questions.explanation: -NO$_2$ strongly withdraws electron density by both $-I$ and $-R$ effects, deactivating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles to the meta position.

questions.q: The relative ease of free-radical halogenation of hydrogens in an alkane follows the order
questions.explanation: The more substituted (3°) radical intermediate is more stable due to greater hyperconjugation/+I effect, so 3° C-H bonds are abstracted fastest: 3° > 2° > 1°.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon with molecular formula C$_5$H$_8$ belongs to which homologous series (assuming one degree of unsaturation type, acyclic)?
questions.explanation: General formula for alkynes/dienes is C$_n$H$_{2n-2}$; for n = 5, $2(5)-2 = 8$, matching C$_5$H$_8$.

questions.q: Complete combustion of 1 mole of propane (C$_3$H$_8$) requires how many moles of O$_2$?
questions.explanation: C$_3$H$_8 + 5O_2 \to 3CO_2 + 4H_2O$; balancing O atoms: $3\times2 + 4\times1 = 10$ O atoms $= 5$ O$_2$ molecules.

questions.q: Dehydration of 2-methylbutan-2-ol with conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ gives predominantly (Zaitsev product)
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule favours the more substituted (more stable) alkene; removal of H from the more substituted adjacent carbon gives 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product.

questions.q: Which alkyne reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas?
questions.explanation: Terminal alkynes have an acidic $\equiv$C-H (sp carbon), reacting with active metals like Na to liberate H$_2$ and form sodium acetylide-type salts; internal alkynes lack this acidic hydrogen.

questions.q: Markovnikov's rule for addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene states that
options: H adds to the carbon bearing fewer hydrogens
H and X add randomly with equal probability
X (halogen) adds to the carbon bearing fewer hydrogens, via the more stable carbocation intermediate
the reaction proceeds only via a free-radical mechanism
questions.explanation: The proton adds first to give the more stable (more substituted) carbocation, so the halide ion then bonds to the carbon that originally had fewer H atoms.

questions.q: Which of these is an ortho/para-directing but deactivating substituent on benzene?
questions.explanation: Halogens withdraw electron density inductively ($-I$, deactivating the ring overall) but can donate a lone pair by resonance ($+R$) into the ortho/para positions specifically, making them o,p-directing yet deactivating.

questions.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with CH$_3$COCl/anhydrous AlCl$_3$ gives
questions.explanation: The acylium ion CH$_3$CO$^+$ generated from CH$_3$COCl/AlCl$_3$ substitutes onto the benzene ring to give the aryl ketone, acetophenone.

questions.q: 5.6 litres of an alkene at STP weighs 10.5 g. The alkene is
questions.explanation: Moles $= 5.6/22.4 = 0.25$. Molar mass $= 10.5/0.25 = 42$ g mol$^{-1}$. For C$_nH_{2n}$, $14n = 42 \Rightarrow n = 3$, i.e. propene (C$_3$H$_6$).

questions.q: The number of moles of Br$_2$ required to completely saturate 1 mole of hex-1-yne (via addition) is
questions.explanation: A triple bond adds two molecules of Br$_2$ sequentially (via the alkene dibromide intermediate) to give the tetrabromide, so 2 mol Br$_2$ are needed per mole of alkyne.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about benzene's resonance energy is correct?
options: It is negative, showing benzene is less stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene
Its resonance energy ($\approx$152 kJ mol$^{-1}$) is the difference between the calculated (hypothetical Kekulé) and experimental heats of hydrogenation
It has zero resonance energy since it is fully conjugated
It equals the heat of hydrogenation of cyclohexene
questions.explanation: Resonance energy is the extra stability of the real delocalised benzene compared to the hypothetical Kekulé (cyclohexatriene) structure, measured as the difference between expected and observed heats of hydrogenation (about 152 kJ mol$^{-1}$).

questions.q: Wurtz-Fittig reaction of a mixture of bromobenzene and methyl bromide with sodium in dry ether gives mainly
questions.explanation: Wurtz-Fittig reaction couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide using sodium, joining the aryl and alkyl groups: C$_6$H$_5$Br + CH$_3$Br + 2Na $\to$ C$_6$H$_5$CH$_3$ (toluene) + 2NaBr.

questions.q: Electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium acetate (Kolbe's electrolysis) produces
options: ethane at the anode, with CO$_2$ and H$_2$ at cathode/anode
questions.explanation: At the anode, acetate ions are oxidised: $2CH_3COO^- \to C_2H_6 + 2CO_2 + 2e^-$, giving ethane and CO$_2$ at the anode, while H$_2$ is liberated at the cathode.

questions.q: The correct order of acidic character of the C-H bond (ease of removing a proton) is
questions.explanation: Greater s-character of the C-H bond holds the bonding electrons closer to carbon, making the H more easily removed as H$^+$; s-character is sp (50%) > sp$^2$ (33%) > sp$^3$ (25%), so terminal alkyne > alkene > alkane in acidity.

questions.q: Treatment of an alkene with cold, dilute alkaline KMnO$_4$ (Baeyer's reagent) gives
options: a vicinal diol (syn-dihydroxylation) and decolorises the purple colour
questions.explanation: Baeyer's reagent (cold dilute alkaline KMnO$_4$) adds two -OH groups across the double bond to give a cis-diol, and the purple colour of KMnO$_4$ fades — a classic test for unsaturation.

questions.q: Bromine water is used as a simple test to distinguish an alkane from an alkene because
options: alkenes rapidly decolorise the orange bromine water by addition, while alkanes do not react under these conditions
alkanes decolorise it faster than alkenes
questions.explanation: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with Br$_2$, decolorising bromine water; saturated alkanes have no $\pi$ bond and do not react under these mild conditions.

questions.q: Complete catalytic hydrogenation of one mole of an alkyne (R-C$\equiv$C-R') to the corresponding alkane requires
questions.explanation: The triple bond first adds 1 mol H$_2$ to give an alkene, which adds a further 1 mol H$_2$ to give the alkane — 2 mol H$_2$ in total.

questions.q: The number of moles of O$_2$ required for the complete combustion of 2 moles of acetylene (C$_2$H$_2$) is
questions.explanation: $C_2H_2 + \dfrac{5}{2}O_2 \to 2CO_2 + H_2O$; for 1 mol C$_2$H$_2$, 2.5 mol O$_2$ is needed, so 2 mol C$_2$H$_2$ requires $2\times2.5 = 5$ mol O$_2$.

questions.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation fails when carried out directly on
questions.explanation: Strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene lack sufficient electron density to attack the electrophilic alkyl carbocation/AlCl$_3$ complex, so Friedel-Crafts reactions do not proceed on nitrobenzene (or other strongly deactivated arenes).

questions.q: A major limitation of Friedel-Crafts alkylation is that
options: the product ring becomes more activated towards further substitution, often leading to polyalkylation
it never forms a carbocation intermediate
it cannot use AlCl$_3$ as catalyst
it only works on aliphatic compounds
questions.explanation: Since alkyl groups are electron-donating (activating), the monoalkylated product is more reactive than benzene itself towards further electrophilic attack, commonly giving a mixture of polyalkylated products.

questions.q: Ozonolysis of an alkene, followed by Zn/H$_2$O work-up, gives only acetone [(CH$_3$)$_2$C=O] as the sole product. The original alkene must have been
questions.explanation: Getting only one carbonyl product means the alkene was symmetrical about the double bond, with identical groups on both carbons; (CH$_3$)$_2$C=C(CH$_3$)$_2$ cleaves to give two identical molecules of acetone.

questions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane requires
options: Ni catalyst under high temperature and pressure (with H$_2$)
questions.explanation: Because of its aromatic stability, benzene requires more forcing conditions (Ni catalyst, high temperature and pressure) to add 3 mol H$_2$ and form cyclohexane, unlike simple alkenes.

questions.q: Benzenesulphonic acid (from sulphonation of benzene with fuming H$_2$SO$_4$) can be converted back to benzene by
options: treatment with NaOH followed by CaO
questions.explanation: Sulphonation is reversible; heating benzenesulphonic acid with dilute sulphuric acid or steam hydrolyses off the -SO$_3$H group, regenerating benzene.

questions.q: The number of possible structural (chain) isomers of hexane, C$_6$H$_{14}$, is
questions.explanation: Hexane has 5 structural isomers: n-hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,3-dimethylbutane and 2,2-dimethylbutane.

questions.q: Thermal or catalytic cracking of higher alkanes (as in petroleum refining) mainly produces
options: smaller alkanes and alkenes by breaking C-C bonds
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks C-C bonds in large alkane molecules (from petroleum) under heat/catalyst to give a mixture of smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes, e.g. for petrol and petrochemical feedstocks.

questions.q: 2.24 L of a gaseous alkane at STP weighs 4.4 g. The alkane is
Which of the following alkenes does NOT show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?
questions.explanation: In propene, one of the doubly bonded carbons bears two identical hydrogen atoms, so it does not satisfy the requirement (two different groups on each sp$^2$ carbon) for cis-trans isomerism.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon with molecular formula C$_4$H$_6$ belongs to which class (2 degrees of unsaturation, acyclic, one type)?
questions.explanation: C$_nH_{2n-2}$ is the general formula for alkynes and dienes; for n = 4, $2(4)-2 = 6$, matching C$_4$H$_6$ (e.g. but-1-yne or buta-1,3-diene).

questions.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation is often preferred over alkylation for introducing a side chain on benzene because
options: the acylium ion does not rearrange, avoiding the carbocation rearrangements seen in alkylation, and prevents polysubstitution since the product ketone is deactivated
acylation does not require a catalyst
questions.explanation: The resonance-stabilised acylium ion (RCO$^+$) does not undergo skeletal rearrangement, and the carbonyl product deactivates the ring, preventing further substitution — both advantages over alkylation.

questions.q: The volume of O$_2$ (at STP) required for the complete combustion of 2.24 L of ethane (C$_2$H$_6$) at STP is
questions.explanation: $C_2H_6 + \dfrac{7}{2}O_2 \to 2CO_2 + 3H_2O$. Moles of ethane $= 2.24/22.4 = 0.1$; moles O$_2$ needed $= 0.1\times3.5 = 0.35$ mol $= 0.35\times22.4 = 7.84$ L at STP.

questions.q: Unlike alkenes, benzene does NOT readily decolorise bromine water at room temperature because
options: the delocalised, resonance-stabilised aromatic system makes addition reactions (which would destroy this stability) much less favourable than substitution
questions.explanation: Addition across a C=C in benzene would disrupt its aromatic delocalisation and resonance stabilisation, so benzene preferentially undergoes electrophilic substitution (retaining aromaticity) rather than addition, unlike simple alkenes.
